The FinTech sector in the Middle East is growing rapidly with a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 30%.

“The Middle East has seen significant growth as a FinTech hub both for investors and tech-savvy innovators.”

In the Middle East, countries such as Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia have displayed public interest in this trend.

Before the explosion of FinTech in the Middle East, seeking regulatory approvals and building the proper IT infrastructure to offer financial services was extremely costly and timely.

Despite all the advancements, the FinTech ecosystem in the Middle East still faces obstacles limiting its growth. In addition, while many banks in the Middle East are engaging with FinTechs in exploratory projects and intense discussions, so far there have been few strategic partnerships.

In a Deloitte study of the relationship between digital leaders and FinTechs in the Middle East, only 5% of banks partnered to win while 15% partnered to differentiate. This means that banks in the Middle East are engaging with FinTechs in exploratory projects and intense discussions, but limited strategic partnerships.

web.description:
We understood from day one that this was going to be difficult.

But cross-border payments are somewhat marginal to the business model of most of the companies which provide this service. Indeed, each major corridor sometimes seems to behave like its own market, with distinct frictions. And so on.

Secondly, we face what I might call ‘exogenous dependencies’: for example, it has become clear that cross-border payments rely heavily on foreign exchange markets which are the largest markets in the world and outside the remit of our roadmap.

On the one hand, it seems, we may not be able to rely as much as we hoped on competitive markets to resolve issues, even if we do everything we can to make space for competition to work as well as it can. Neither the visible nor the invisible hand seems to have a strong grip on this issue.

But it is far from hopeless.

In contrast, the volume of cross-border payments being made by stablecoins is estimated to be only a fraction of this – by some estimates less than 0.2 per cent of total cross border payments in 2025. But neither is more than a possibility at this point.

The work has not just been about getting better policy frameworks, it has also been about technical frictions.
